title: Nuclear veteran says investigation a 'magical moment'

input.evidence_text: Nuclear veteran says investigation a 'magical moment' - BBC News Image caption, John Morris has long campaigned for a study into the health impacts of Britain's nuclear programme By Richard Baker North West Published 26 November 2026 A nuclear test veteran who developed cancer and lost his four-month-old son, has said hearing an independent panel will look into Britain's atomic programme was "a magical moment". John Morris, from Rochdale, was sent to Christmas Island in the 1950s to work on the UK's growing nuclear programme - and now believes the loss of his son was due to radiation exposure picked up on the island. It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced an investigation into the lasting health impacts of testing exercises in the 1950s and 60s. Morris, who alongside fellow veterans have long campaigned for an investigation, said this announcement feels different "without a shadow of a doubt". "He [Burnham] has delivered something that has taken more than 70 years to come to fruition, I can't thank you enough," Morris told BBC North West Tonight . Image caption, Burnham told campaigners in Downing Street that he would launch an independent investigation Morris said he was 18 when he was sent to Christmas Island, in the Pacific Ocean, to work as a laundry operator on a British nuclear site. The island was a major Anglo American nuclear site in the Cold War period, lying just north of Australia. "I thought we were helping soldiers build a runway, I have no idea why, and suddenly we found out we were testing atomic bombs," Morris said. He said safety concerns when a blast went off were relaxed, with him being told to turn his back to the explosion and cover his eyes. input.summary: Jacqui Carroll wanted to help other working class people gain experience in the industry
input.evidence_text: The film company in Manchester that started with £50 and a camera - BBC News Image caption, Jacqui Carroll wanted to give aspiring film makers new opportunities By Kelly Foran North West Published 26 November 2026 In 2001, Jacqui Carroll and Terry Egan started a film and documentary company from their home with just £50, a digital video camera and a belief that everyone has a story worth telling. Now, a quarter of a century later, the stories captured on film will form part of the North West Film Archive. REELMCR was set up to help other working class people gain opportunities and experience in an industry that Jacqui said always felt like it was for a "different class". "When I was in school I said I wanted to be an actor or an astronaut and was laughed at," she said. "I was told I could be a receptionist and that's what I ended up doing. "When I was 39 and pregnant with my daughter I had to stay in and watch TV. "That's when I realised there was nobody who sounded like me and people I knew on TV. "Even in the soaps they were putting the accents on." Image caption, Terry Egan said he felt the biggest amount of pride when the people involved watched their work Jacqui and Terry decided to set up the company in Manchester making films and documentaries as well as providing training and projects in working-class communities. From the sound engineers to the scriptwriters, everyone involved was given a chance to shine. "I was a reader and got my education in other ways," said Terry, who admits he did not attend school. "But ReelMCR... it would have been just what I needed when I was growing up. "It would have made my life easier." input.summary: The prime minister vowed to get people off the streets by Christmas when he entered Downing Street
input.evidence_text: Homeless charity says 'no change' in Manchester rough sleeping despite PM's pledge - BBC News Image caption, Dave Evans co-founded a homeless charity to help support those in need By Anna Jameson and Lauren Hirst , North West Published 26 November 2026 A homeless charity's co-founder has said he fears Andy Burnham will not be able to meet his pledge to end rough sleeping as the number of those sleeping on the streets in Manchester continues to rise. When he entered Downing Street in the summer, the prime minister pledged to provide a route out of rough sleeping by Christmas through a £442m package of emergency accommodation and practical support over three years. A further £432m was added to the scheme in October. However, with just weeks to go until Christmas, Dave Evans, from the Two Brews charity, said he believed rough sleeping had "gone up dramatically" as he witnessed the daily struggle of those on the streets. When Burnham was first elected as the Mayor of Greater Manchester in May 2017, he made the same pledge to end the need for rough sleeping across all 10 boroughs. He made a great start with the number of rough sleepers in Greater Manchester reducing during the pandemic to 89 in 2021 from 268 in 2017. But over the last five years, numbers have been creeping up. The latest annual rough sleeping snapshot, where local authorities in England provide a figure on any one night in Autumn, shows Greater Manchester has 197 rough sleepers, 43 more than in 2024. The figures for 2026 are expected early next year. 'Big increase' Jordan Parker, from Two Brews, said he and Evans had started the charity six years ago. Nine defendants are on trial in the case. The northbound section of Alan Turing Way, in Beswick close to the Etihad Stadium , was shut off in March after a suspected sinkhole was discovered For months the council wasn’t entirely sure what had caused the stretch of road to collapse. But in September, engineers discovered it was a 50m-deep mineshaft under the road that triggered the 3m-wide crater There is a long history of mining and colliers throughout east Manchester, but this mineshaft wasn’t recorded on historic maps and took workers by surprise. Further investigations revealed the extent of the cavity and scale of repairs required In order to stabilise the shaft, contractors filled it with 120 tonnes of concrete grout before putting a ‘reinforced concrete slab’ over the top. Concrete has also been used to 'backfill' the original excavation with utilities pipes, and the road surface, then being restored In an update, Manchester City Council said the 'unprecedented' and 'highly complex' works were 'reaching their conclusion' and that the road would reopen on Saturday, November 28. It is expected to be clear by mid-morning

The northbound section of Alan Turing Way, in Beswick close to the Etihad Stadium , was shut off in March after a suspected sinkhole was discovered For months the council wasn’t entirely sure what had caused the stretch of road to collapse. But in September, engineers discovered it was a 50m-deep mineshaft under the road that triggered the 3m-wide crater There is a long history of mining and colliers throughout east Manchester, but this mineshaft wasn’t recorded on historic maps and took workers by surprise. Further investigations revealed the extent of the cavity and scale of repairs required In order to stabilise the shaft, contractors filled it with 120 tonnes of concrete grout before putting a ‘reinforced concrete slab’ over the top. Concrete has also been used to 'backfill' the original excavation with utilities pipes, and the road surface, then being restored In an update, Manchester City Council said the 'unprecedented' and 'highly complex' works were 'reaching their conclusion' and that the road would reopen on Saturday, November 28. It is expected to be clear by mid-morning
